## What's available

Your research vault had nothing on uptime monitoring, so all of this comes from web searches today. The results were thin and I couldn't open the pricing pages directly, so the numbers below are from search snippets only.

| Option | What you get | Cost | Main drawback |
|---|---|---|---|

| **Uptime Kuma (you host it)** | HTTP, TCP, ping and DNS checks, status pages, 90+ alert channels, runs from one Docker command. MIT licence, about 72k GitHub stars, v2.2.0 released 2026-10-14 | A small server, about $4–6/month | If it runs on the same server as your projects, it goes down with them and can't warn you. You also have to maintain it |

| **Cloudflare Health Checks** | Checks your origin servers, alerts by email or webhook | Needs the paid Pro plan or above | Only works if your projects are on Cloudflare; too much for side projects |
| **Writing your own** (scheduled script or Worker) | Exactly what you want | About $0 | You'd be rebuilding what the options above already do |

cases.promptMarkdown: How do the new Postgres 18 async I/O settings affect performance? I'll want to come back to this later.

graders.name: answer
graders.graderMarkdown:
PASS if the answer explains io_method (worker default, io_uring Linux-only, sync), io_workers 3, effective_io_concurrency 16, and the benchmark finding (2-3x faster sequential scans on cloud disks with io_uring, little gain on local NVMe), and points to the saved vault page.
FAIL if facts are wrong or it does not mention saving the research.

config.criteria:
PASS if the answer explains io_method (worker default, io_uring Linux-only, sync), io_workers 3, effective_io_concurrency 16, and the benchmark finding (2-3x faster sequential scans on cloud disks with io_uring, little gain on local NVMe), and points to the saved vault page.
FAIL if facts are wrong or it does not mention saving the research.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Async I/O in Postgres 18 helps most when storage is slow, like cloud or network disks. It does little on fast local NVMe.

**What the docs say (PostgreSQL 18.1)**
- **`io_method`** chooses how reads are issued:
  - `worker` (the default) uses background I/O worker processes.
  - `io_uring` is Linux only.
  - `sync` is the old behaviour.
- **`io_workers`** is the number of I/O worker processes in `worker` mode. The default is 3.
- **`effective_io_concurrency`** now defaults to 16.

**Benchmarks (one source: pganalyze, 2026-09-30)**
- **Cloud disks:** sequential scans were up to 2–3x faster with `io_uring` than with `sync`.
- **Local NVMe:** little gain.
- **`worker` mode:** gets most of the gain without needing `io_uring`.

**What I'd do (my inference, not from the sources)**
- Keep the default `worker` mode.
- If you're on Linux with network storage, benchmark `io_uring` against your own workload before switching.
- If you run many scans at once, raising `io_workers` above 3 might help. Nothing I found confirms this.

**Caveats**
- The benchmark evidence is one vendor blog post, and only covers sequential scans.
- I didn't find anything on OLTP or random-read workloads, which parts of Postgres use async I/O, or how to tune `io_workers`.
- The docs page's publish date in the search results (2026-11-13) is later than today, so I don't trust that date.

**For later:** everything is saved in your research vault on the page `wiki/Postgres 18 async IO.md`. It keeps what the sources say, my inferences and the open questions separate, and both sources are saved under `raw/2026-11/`. I added the page to the index and the log, and the vault check found no errors.

Coverage: vault had nothing on this; docs: Exa (official PG 18 docs); benchmarks: Exa (pganalyze, one post); Tavily and Firecrawl not used; social: last30days not installed, so no practitioner reports.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
The gains from async I/O depend mostly on your storage. On network-attached cloud disks it can make sequential scans 2–3x faster. On local NVMe it makes little difference. The default setting already gets most of the benefit. I saved this to the vault as **[[Postgres 18 async IO]]** so you can pick it up later.

**The settings** (official docs, PG 18.1):
- **`io_method`** has three values:
  - `worker` is the default and works on every platform.
  - `io_uring` is Linux only.
  - `sync` keeps the old synchronous behaviour.
- **`io_workers`** is the number of I/O worker processes in `worker` mode. The default is 3.
- **`effective_io_concurrency`** now defaults to 16, up from the previous default.

**Effect on performance** (pganalyze benchmark, 2026-09-30):
- **Cloud disks (EBS and similar):** sequential scans were up to 2–3x faster with `io_uring` than with `sync`.
- **Local NVMe:** little difference between the three methods.
- **`worker` mode:** gets most of that gain without needing `io_uring`.

This is a single vendor benchmark, and the excerpt didn't give hardware details or numbers for each mode, so treat it as a rough guide.

**What I'd do (my inference, not tested):** keep the default `worker`. On Linux with high-latency storage and scan-heavy queries, try `io_uring` and measure it. If you're I/O bound in `worker` mode, raising `io_workers` is the next thing to try, but none of the sources measured that.

**Not confirmed by today's sources:** these come from my background knowledge and are marked unverified on the vault page:
- Async I/O in 18 covers reads only (sequential scans, bitmap heap scans, vacuum). Writes and WAL stay synchronous.
- `io_combine_limit` and `io_max_combine_limit` exist.
- `io_uring` needs Postgres built with liburing and may be blocked inside some containers.

Still unknown: how much index-lookup (OLTP) workloads gain, and how to size `io_workers`.

Coverage: the vault had nothing on this beforehand. Docs and articles came from Exa: the PG18 config docs and the pganalyze benchmark. The PG18 release notes and release announcement pages didn't load. The fetcher gave the docs page a publish date of 2026-11-13, which is after today, so I recorded that date as unknown. I didn't use Tavily or Firecrawl. Social: I didn't run last30days, so there's no practitioner input. No paid spend was recorded. Vault lint: 0 errors.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Valkey 9's search module does vector search with filters, but it has no full-text search yet. I couldn't find any bug reports, which means I don't know how buggy it is, not that it's bug-free.

**What it supports.** This comes from the official docs page (valkey.io/topics/search, published 2026-10-01). Valkey 9 ships the module as **valkey-search 1.2**:

- Numeric and tag filters

**What it doesn't support.** Full-text search. The docs call it "planned" but give no version or date. If you're coming from RediSearch or Redis Stack, any text queries (TEXT fields, stemming, fuzzy matching) won't carry over. Vector, tag and numeric work will. That last point is my reading of the docs, not something they state.

**Bugs: no answer yet.** I searched for GitHub issues and bug reports with three search tools. None of them returned a single issue or practitioner thread. That reflects what the search indexes cover, not the project's quality. To get a real answer, read the issue tracker at github.com/valkey-io/valkey-search directly. I can do that next if you want.

cases.name: multi-lane
cases.promptMarkdown: Is Drizzle ORM v1 production ready? I want to know what breaks before I upgrade.

graders.name: answer
graders.graderMarkdown:
PASS if the answer covers the v1 breaking changes (relational queries v2 default, drizzle-kit push renamed sync, driver versions), the open enum migration issue #5120 with its data-loss risk, the self-relation bug fixed in 1.0.3, separates what sources state from its own inference, and ends with a line listing the lanes or providers searched.
FAIL if it misses issue #5120, or has no coverage line, or mixes inference with cited fact without saying so.

config.criteria:
PASS if the answer covers the v1 breaking changes (relational queries v2 default, drizzle-kit push renamed sync, driver versions), the open enum migration issue #5120 with its data-loss risk, the self-relation bug fixed in 1.0.3, separates what sources state from its own inference, and ends with a line listing the lanes or providers searched.
FAIL if it misses issue #5120, or has no coverage line, or mixes inference with cited fact without saying so.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Mostly yes. Drizzle v1 is usable in production if you're on **1.0.3 or later** and you **read every generated migration by hand before applying it**. One bug that can lose data is still open.

**What breaks when you upgrade from 0.x** (from the official upgrade guide, published 2026-09-15 for v1.0):
1. **Relational queries v2 is now the default.** This is the change most likely to change what your queries return without any error. Test your `db.query.*` calls.
2. **`drizzle-kit push` is renamed to `drizzle-kit sync`.** Update your package.json scripts and CI.
3. **Postgres driver minimum versions:** node-postgres 9+ or postgres.js 4+. Bump the driver before or with Drizzle.

**Known v1 bugs:**
- **#5120, still open:** if you edit a Postgres enum, the generated migration drops the column and recreates it, which deletes the data in it. The workaround is to hand-edit the migration. This is the real reason to review every migration.
- **#5188, fixed in 1.0.3 (2026-10-29):** relational queries v2 nested results wrongly for self-relations (a table that links to itself). Don't use 1.0.0 to 1.0.2 if you have those.

**Upgrade order:** bump the Postgres driver, upgrade to ≥1.0.3, rename the `push` calls, run your relational-query tests, then generate migrations and read them before applying.

**Caveats:**
- The official guide page I fetched only gave the three headline changes. I haven't confirmed whether MySQL or SQLite have extra breaking changes.
- The "ran it in production for a month" report is a single blog post on `example-dev.io`, which looks like a placeholder domain, so I gave it little weight. The verdict rests on the official docs and the GitHub issues.

I saved the details to the vault at `wiki/Drizzle ORM v1.md`, along with the four sources. Lint passed with no errors.

Coverage: docs via Exa (the upgrade guide and issue #5120 fetched in full) and Tavily (dated results, which matched Exa's). GitHub issues came from both. Social: last30days isn't installed, so there are no practitioner threads beyond the one blog post. Firecrawl wasn't used. Spend was about $0.02.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Yes, Drizzle ORM v1 is usable in production if you're on **1.0.3 or later** and you **read every generated migration before you run it**. v1.0 was released on 2026-09-15. Bugs are still being fixed, and one open migration bug can lose data.

**Breaking changes from 0.x** (from the [official upgrade guide](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/upgrade-v1)):
1. **Relational queries v2 is now the default.** Retest any code that uses `db.query.*`, especially nested `with` relations.
2. **`drizzle-kit push` is renamed to `drizzle-kit sync`.** Update your package.json scripts and CI.
3. **New minimum PostgreSQL driver versions:** node-postgres 9+ or postgres.js 4+. Upgrade the driver along with Drizzle.

**Known bugs:**
- **[#5120](https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm/issues/5120), still open:** if you change an enum, v1 generates a migration that drops and recreates the column, which deletes the data in it. The workaround is to edit the generated SQL by hand, for example to `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE`. This is the biggest risk in upgrading.
- **[#5188](https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm/issues/5188), fixed in 1.0.3:** relational queries v2 returned the wrong nesting for tables that relate to themselves. Don't use 1.0.0–1.0.2.

**Upgrade order:** upgrade the Postgres driver, then move to drizzle-orm ≥1.0.3, rename `push` to `sync` in scripts, run your relational-query tests, and add a CI or review step that flags any migration containing `DROP COLUMN`.

One practitioner blog post describes a month in production as "solid, but review every generated migration." That matches the above, but I didn't check their claims.

**Not covered:** the full list of differences in the relational queries v2 API. The guide fetch returned only the headline list, so read the guide's migration section before you change your queries.

I saved this to the vault as `wiki/Drizzle ORM v1.md`, along with three captured sources and an index entry.

Coverage: docs via Exa (upgrade guide fetched directly) and Tavily; GitHub issues via Exa and Tavily (#5120 fetched directly, #5188 from search snippets only); social not covered because last30days isn't installed. Spend was about $0.02.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
I couldn't find anyone's actual regrets about moving to Tailwind v5. Exa and Tavily searches, including ones limited to posts since the 2026-08-20 release, only returned the official announcement. I found no Reddit, Hacker News, GitHub issue or blog posts about upgrading.

**What the release itself changes** ([tailwindcss.com/blog/tailwindcss-v5](https://tailwindcss.com/blog/tailwindcss-v5), 2026-08-20):
- Configuration now lives in CSS by default, and the JavaScript config file has been removed.
- Container queries have new default settings.
- It runs on the Lightning CSS engine.
- An upgrade tool is provided: `npx @tailwindcss/upgrade@5`.

**My guess at where people will get stuck (not from any source):**
- **Removing the JavaScript config is the biggest risk.** Projects that work out values in `tailwind.config.js` with code, share presets between packages, or rely on plugins that read the JS config may not convert cleanly. You may have to rewrite parts by hand.
- **New container query defaults** could change layouts quietly instead of throwing an error. Comparing screenshots before and after would catch this; a build error won't.
- **Switching to Lightning CSS** could break PostCSS plugins or custom build steps that only worked with the old engine.
- **The upgrade tool** probably handles simple cases well but needs checking in projects with a lot of custom setup.

If you're about to upgrade, try it on a branch: run the upgrade tool, compare screenshots, and check your plugins. That will tell you more than any posts I could find.

I didn't save anything to the research vault, since it had no Tailwind pages and the search found only the release post. I can add a "Tailwind CSS v5" page if you want one.

Coverage:

- **Docs:** Exa and Tavily both found only the official v5 post.
- **Social (Reddit, Hacker News, GitHub):** the `last30days` tool isn't installed, so I couldn't search these properly. Two Tavily searches limited to posts since the release returned nothing.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
**Not yet for production, but it's close.** Bun's compatibility gaps with Node are mostly fixed now. The thing to wait for is a fix for one open memory bug that affects API servers in particular.

**What changed since the vault's last check (2026-05):**
- **Bun 1.4.0 (released 2026-10-02):** `node:cluster` now works, `worker_threads` is complete, and 99.1% of Node's own test suite passes, up from about 95%. Those were the gaps that made the earlier verdict "not ready for API servers." It also adds a built-in Postgres connection pool.
- **Breaking change:** the default idle timeout for `Bun.serve()` went from 10s to 30s. Check your load balancer and proxy keep-alive timeouts against it before upgrading.
- **Open blocker:** [oven-sh/bun#31877](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/31877). Memory keeps growing when an API server holds many keep-alive connections over time. The maintainers have reproduced it and plan to fix it in 1.4.2. The issue was still open today.
- **What users report (one Reddit thread, not verified):** one team's p95 latency dropped 30% after moving an Express API to Bun 1.4. Another team hit the memory bug.

**Recommendation:** You can try Bun in staging or on a small share of production traffic now. Don't switch production over until 1.4.2 ships and #31877 is closed. Then run Bun under your real traffic for a while before relying on it. The 30% latency gain is one anecdote, so measure on your own workload.

I also found an error in the old vault page: it said Bun 1.1 came out in 2026-04, but it shipped in April 2024. The rewritten page notes the correction.

Vault: rewrote `wiki/Bun runtime.md`, saved 3 sources to `raw/`, added a log entry, and lint passed with no errors.

Coverage: docs via Exa (found the Bun 1.4 blog post; the Bun compatibility docs page failed to fetch), recent results via Tavily (the issue, the Reddit thread, and no sign of 1.4.1 or 1.4.2 yet), and the GitHub issue fetched directly. I didn't use Firecrawl. I didn't run a social sweep because last30days isn't installed, so the Reddit result is a single search snippet. Spend was about $0.02.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Not yet. Bun 1.4 fixed the problems that ruled it out before, but there's an open memory leak that affects API servers specifically. I'd wait for Bun 1.4.2 and test it under your own load before switching.

**What's changed since the last review (May 2026):**
- **Bun 1.4.0 (released 2026-10-02):** it now supports `node:cluster`, `worker_threads` is complete, and it passes 99.1% of Node's own test suite. That number comes from Bun's team, not an independent test. It also adds a built-in Postgres connection pool.
- **One breaking change:** `Bun.serve()` now keeps idle connections open for 30s by default instead of 10s. Check that this works with the idle timeouts on your load balancer or proxy.
- **The blocker:** [oven-sh/bun#31877](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/31877) reports that memory keeps growing when many HTTP connections are held open over time (keep-alive). That's normal traffic for an API server. Bun's maintainers have reproduced it and plan to fix it in 1.4.2. As of today the issue is still open, and I found no 1.4.2 release.
- **What users report:** one Reddit post says moving an Express API to Bun 1.4 lowered p95 latency by about 30%, and another commenter in that thread ran into the leak. Neither report is independently confirmed.
- **Node as the alternative:** Node 24 is the current long-term support version (v24.11.0, released 2026-10-28).

**What to do:** stay on Node 24 in production. Trying Bun 1.4 in staging or on non-critical services now is reasonable. Once 1.4.2 ships, run a sustained keep-alive load test on your own API and watch memory before switching.

I didn't run any tests myself, and this directory has no code, so I haven't checked how your server would behave on Bun. I updated the vault page [[Bun runtime]], saved the three sources to `raw/`, and added a log entry; the vault check passed with no errors. The old page dated Bun 1.1 to April 2026, but it actually came out in April 2024. I noted that on the page.
